content.text: Students extend the unit study of belonging by turning themes from
Look Both Ways
into researchable questions.
Stories about ordinary moments help us see who we are and how we belong; research can deepen our understanding of those moments and communities.
In Lesson 22, students will evaluate the credibility and usefulness of sources connected to the question they generated today.
This inquiry work strengthens students' ability to focus on a meaningful small moment and build ideas they may later draw on in narrative reflection and discussion.
Look Both Ways,
by Jason Reynolds

Turn and Talk
Quick Write

In recent lessons, we have been noticing how Jason Reynolds turns ordinary moments into stories about identity, empathy, and belonging. Today, we are going to take one big unit idea and turn it into a question we can actually research. That matters because strong questions help with our next step: finding strong sources.
Which unit idea feels broad enough that we could learn more about through research: belonging, voice, friendship, routines, empathy, or community? What makes it worth studying?
Directions:
Take 30 seconds to think, then turn to a partner. Partner A shares first, then Partner B. Be ready to name one idea you think could become a research topic.
When a research topic is too big, the answers get vague or hard to find. The smart move is to narrow the topic step by step until it becomes a question that sources can help answer.
Why is the question “How do after-school clubs help middle school students feel a stronger sense of belonging?” stronger than the question “Why is belonging important?”
How can you tell whether a question is researchable instead of just interesting?
Check for Understanding
Write one broad topic, one narrowed topic, and one draft question that begins with how or why.

student.title: Literacy Lab: Inquiry Protocol — Focus & Frame

content.text: Part A: Narrow Your Topic
Directions:

Choose a broad topic connected to our unit, such as belonging, voice, empathy, school routines, friendship, storytelling, or community. You may connect your topic to something you have experienced if you want to, but you can also stay fully with the book, our class discussions, and the ideas we have studied. Use the organizer to work through Activate, Narrow, Question, and Check.
What broad topic did you choose, and how did you narrow it?
Is your draft question something a source could answer, or is it mostly asking for an opinion? How do you know?
Check for Understanding
Show a partner the point on your organizer where your topic became specific enough to research. Explain what you changed.
Part B: Frame Keywords and Find One Likely Source
Turn and Talk
Directions:

Now test your question like a researcher. Write 3-5 keywords you could use to search for information. Then use the source set to find one source that seems relevant to your question right now. You are not proving it is perfect yet; you are identifying one source that looks like a promising match.
Which keywords gave you the most useful results, and how do you know?
Which source seems most relevant to your question right now? What in the title, subtitle, or preview makes you think that?
Directions:
Turn to a partner and explain your best keyword choice and your likely source. Your partner should listen for whether the source really matches the question or only matches one word from it.
Pulse Check
Which question is the most focused and researchable?
A. Why is community important?
B. What do students do after school?
C. How do after-school routines help middle school students feel like they belong at school?
D. What is the best story about middle school ever written?
Directions:
Use your organizer and notes to reflect on today's research moves. Answer all parts of the question so you leave with a clear plan for our next lesson.
Think-Pair-Share
Use this brief routine to connect the unit's reading work to today's inquiry work. Students should hear that research begins with curiosity, but strong research also requires focus.
Say these Directions:

In recent lessons, we have been noticing how Jason Reynolds turns ordinary moments into stories about identity, empathy, and belonging. Today, we are going to take one big unit idea and turn it into a question we can actually research. That matters because strong questions help with our next step: finding strong sources.
Ask:
Which unit idea feels broad enough that we could learn more about through research: belonging, voice, friendship, routines, empathy, or community? What makes it worth studying?
Belonging feels worth studying because it shows up in a lot of the book, but it is also big enough that I could learn more about how schools and friendships help people feel included.
Say these Directions:
Take 30 seconds to think, then turn to a partner. Partner A shares first, then Partner B. Be ready to name one idea you think could become a research topic.
Connection to Today's Learning:
Today we are learning that researchers do not stop with a big idea. They shrink it, test it, and make sure it can be answered with real sources.
Students connect the unit's study of belonging and voice to the work of asking focused research questions.
Inquiry Protocol: Focus & Frame
In this investigation, keep the same teacher model topic across research lessons so students can see the process build over time. The teacher model topic for this lesson sequence is
after-school clubs and belonging
Say these Directions:
When a research topic is too big, the answers get vague or hard to find. The smart move is to narrow the topic step by step until it becomes a question that sources can help answer.
Teach: Inquiry Protocol — Focus & Frame

I want to research belonging, but that topic is much too broad. So I ask myself what part of belonging I can actually picture, name, and search for. When I narrow it to after-school clubs and middle school students, I can ask a how or why question instead of a giant question like “What is belonging?” Then I test the question by asking whether articles, websites, interviews, or surveys could help answer it. If the answer is yes, I have a researchable question.
Display the completed model:
Activate—What do I already know about this topic?:
In
Look Both Ways

, ordinary after-school moments reveal friendship, worry, humor, and belonging. I also know that routines and shared spaces can make people feel included or left out, but after-school clubs are a way for students to find people with similar interests.
Narrow—What specific ideas or connections do I want to explore?:
belonging in middle school → school routines → after-school routines →places that help people feel included → school clubs → gaining a sense of belonging at after-school clubs
Question—How can I phrase this as a how or why question?:
How do after-school clubs help middle school students feel a stronger sense of belonging?
Check—Can this question be answered with sources that exist?:
This question is focused and researchable because I could find articles, youth essays, interviews, school websites, and school-community sources or surveys about student participation.
Frame—What keywords or search terms will help me find sources?:
after-school clubs; middle school belonging; shared interests and friendship teens; school club community connection
Ask:
Why is the question “How do after-school clubs help middle school students feel a stronger sense of belonging?” stronger than the question “Why is belonging important?”
The question got stronger because it stopped being about everything connected to belonging and focused on one part of it. That makes it easier to search for sources and easier to answer.
Ask:
How can you tell whether a question is researchable instead of just interesting?

A question is researchable if I can imagine what kinds of sources would answer it. If I cannot think of keywords, sources, or facts I would need, then the question is probably still too broad or too opinion-based.
Support students in using academic language to move from a broad idea to a focused, searchable research question.
Affirm student-generated vocabulary from their own reading, speaking, and lived school knowledge as valuable starting points for inquiry.
Invite students to talk through possible topics in a shared home language before saying or writing the narrowed version in English.
Model the shift from everyday language to research language by naming the exact move: broad topic, narrowed focus, question, check, frame.
Press students to explain why a question is researchable by naming possible source types, not just saying it is a “good question.”
“You said, ‘It’s about clubs and stuff’ — we can explain that by saying, ‘My narrowed topic is how clubs can support middle school students and belonging after school.’”
“That idea connects to researchable because a question is researchable when sources can help answer it.”
Generative Oral/Language Supports (available to all students):
My broad topic is ___, but I can narrow it to ___.
My question asks how/why ___.
This question is researchable because I could use ___ sources.
If students give a yes/no question → Prompt: “Try starting with how or why so the answer has to be explained, not just chosen.”
If students name a broad topic but cannot narrow it → Prompt: “Add a place, a group, or a time frame. What smaller part of this topic could you actually search for?”
Student uses language such as broad topic, narrow, question, and researchable accurately in speech or notes.
Student revises from a vague topic statement toward a searchable how or why question.
Check for Understanding (W.6.7)
Write one broad topic, one narrowed topic, and one draft question that begins with how or why.
How do school lunch routines help sixth graders build friendships during their first months of middle school?
Connection to Today's Learning:
Now students will use the same five moves on a topic connected to the unit's study of voice, identity, and belonging.

teacher.title: Literacy Lab: Inquiry Protocol — Focus & Frame

content.text: Students learn the Inquiry Protocol: Focus & Frame and see a teacher model of moving from a broad topic to a focused, searchable question.
Learning in Action A: Narrow Your Topic (W.6.7)
(15 minutes)
Inquiry Protocol: Focus & Frame
Say these Directions:

Choose a broad topic connected to our unit, such as belonging, voice, empathy, school routines, friendship, storytelling, or community. You may connect your topic to something you have experienced if you want to, but you can also stay fully with the book, our class discussions, and the ideas we have studied. Use the organizer to work through Activate, Narrow, Question, and Check.
Display a completed sample if needed:
Move
Sample Entry
Activate
In our unit, I have noticed that community spaces can shape whether people feel included.
Narrow
school community → belonging →places that help people feel included → after-school clubs
Question
How do after-school clubs help middle school students feel a stronger sense of belonging?
Check
I could answer this with articles, interviews, or school-related sources.
Circulate and use research reflection prompts as students work:
What do you already know about this topic?
Which part of the topic matters most?
What would a source need to tell you?
What needs to get smaller in your question?
Ask:
What broad topic did you choose, and how did you narrow it?

I chose the broad topic of friendship. Then I narrowed it to how school routines can give kids a chance to make friends. Then I narrowed it again to the question “How does the routine of shared lunch at school help students develop friendships?”
Ask:
Is your draft question something a source could answer, or is it mostly asking for an opinion? How do you know?

My question is something a source could answer because I am asking about the impact of sharing a routine on friendship and feeling included. A source could give examples, interviews, or studies about shared routines.
Support students in explaining their topic choices and revising a broad idea into a focused research question.
Honor students' background knowledge about school communities as valid prior knowledge while keeping research anchored in evidence, not disclosure.
Invite students to start with unit language they already own from discussion, including words like belonging, voice, routine, and empathy, before refining them into academic phrases.
Invite students to justify revisions aloud using “because” so they practice reasoning, not just rewriting.
You said "I made it smaller" — we can say "I narrowed my topic to one specific part of belonging."
You said "sources could help" — we can say "This question is searchable because a source could provide examples, facts, or perspectives about it."
Generative Oral/Language Supports:
I narrowed my topic from ___ to ___.
My question is focused because it asks about ___, not everything about ___.
I still need to revise ___ so the question can be answered with sources.
If a student's topic stays too wide, ask them to box the most important noun phrase and remove extra ideas.
If a student writes a yes/no question → _Prompt:_ "Change it into a how or why question so the answer needs explanation."
If a student keeps adding too many ideas into one question → _Prompt:_ "Which idea matters most? Keep that one and cross out the rest for now."
Student explains how the topic became narrower from one draft to the next.
Student avoids vague or opinion-only wording and moves toward a focused, answerable question.
Check for Understanding (W.6.7)
Show a partner the point on your organizer where your topic became specific enough to research. Explain what you changed.
My topic became specific enough between the Narrow step and the Question step, because asking how or why helped me think about what I really wanted to know.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with

narrowing a topic: Offer a three-step verbal ladder: My big topic is ___. One part of that topic is ___. The part I want to study is ___. Then have students turn that last phrase into a how or why question. turning a topic into a question: Provide the frame How does ___ affect ___ in middle school? or Why does ___ matter for ___? written expression: Allow students to talk through their topic and question with the teacher or a partner first, then record it in writing or with speech-to-text.
Ready for extension
Revise the draft question twice and explain which version is strongest and why. Ask students to generate three keyword combinations before moving to Part B.
Learning in Action B: Frame Keywords and Find One Likely Source (W.6.7)
(15 minutes)
Turn and Talk
Say these Directions:

Now test your question like a researcher. Write 3-5 keywords you could use to search for information. Then use the source set to find one source that seems relevant to your question right now. You are not proving it is perfect yet; you are identifying one source that looks like a promising match.
Students may use a curated digital set, article cards, or printouts. Emphasize that today's goal is relevance, not full evaluation; full source evaluation comes in Lesson 40.
Ask:
Which keywords gave you the most useful results, and how do you know?
The keywords that worked best were walk home, students shared routines, and after-school belonging because they matched the main ideas in my question.
Ask:
Which source seems most relevant to your question right now? What in the title, subtitle, or preview makes you think that?

The source I found that focuses on school lunch and socialization seems most relevant to my question. It looks useful because the title mentions school lunches, and the preview says it includes students’ experiences interacting during lunch in middle school.
Say these Directions:
Turn to a partner and explain your best keyword choice and your likely source. Your partner should listen for whether the source really matches the question or only matches one word from it.
Support students in orally justifying why a keyword set or source is relevant to a research question.
Affirm that students who notice patterns in titles and previews are already using strong real-world media literacy skills.
Encourage students to generate everyday search language first, then revise into more academic keywords.
Prompt students to explain relevance with evidence from the title, subtitle, author line, or preview text.
Distinguish between a source that shares one topic word and a source that actually addresses the question's focus.
You said "this one kind of matches" — we can say "This source seems relevant because its title directly addresses my focus on routines and belonging."
You said "I used better words" — we can say "I revised my keywords so the search results would be more closely related to my research question."
Generative Oral/Language Supports:
The keyword ___ helped because ___.
This source seems relevant because it focuses on ___.
I would keep this source/change this source because ___.
If a student chooses a source based on one repeated word only → _Prompt:_ "Does the source match the whole question or just one word from it?"
If a student's keywords are too general → _Prompt:_ "Add one more specific term, such as the age group, place, or activity you are studying."
Student names at least one keyword that closely matches the focused question.
Student justifies a source choice with a specific feature from the source rather than a vague statement such as “It looks good.”
Pulse Check (W.6.7)
Which question is the most focused and researchable?
A. Why is community important?
Incorrect: This is too broad and could lead to general opinions instead of a manageable research path.
B. What do students do after school?
Incorrect: This is somewhat related, but it is still wide and does not name a specific angle or purpose for the research.
C. How do after-school routines help middle school students feel like they belong at school?
Correct: This question is specific, names a clear group, and could be answered with articles, interviews, or school-community sources.
D. What is the best story about middle school ever written?
Incorrect: This is mostly opinion-based and would not lead to a clear evidence-based research investigation.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with

choosing keywords: Have students pull key nouns directly from their question and list them first, then add one more specific word such as middle school, friendship, or belonging. identifying a relevant source: Ask students to compare the question and source title side by side and say, “This source matches my question because both mention ___.” processing and output: Allow students to give an oral explanation of why a source seems relevant before writing the explanation down.
Ready for extension
Try two different keyword sets and compare which one produced more precise results. Find a second source and explain which of the two looks more relevant and why.
Part A: Narrow Your Topic (W.6.7)
Students apply Activate, Narrow, Question, and Check to develop a focused research question.
Part B: Frame Keywords and Find One Likely Source (W.6.7)
Students generate keywords, test them with a source set, and identify one source that seems relevant.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
Use your organizer and notes to reflect on today's research moves. Answer all parts of the question so you leave with a clear plan for our next lesson.
Prompt:
What is your research question, why is it searchable, and what are your next steps based on the source or keywords you found today?

My research question is: “How does the routine of shared lunch at school help students develop friendships?” It is searchable because I can use keywords like ‘middle school friendships,’ ‘cafeteria lunch,’ and ‘shared routines’ to find articles and interviews. My next step is to keep the source I found about school lunches and test one more keyword set so I can see if I can find an even closer match.
Students reflect on the quality of their question, the usefulness of their keywords, and their next research step.
Instruct students to:
Record your final research question and 3-5 keywords in your journal. If you have access to your source from class, bring back its title or link for Lesson 40.

data.subject: ELA

standards.description: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and refocusing the inquiry when appropriate.
Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.

Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess the credibility of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and providing basic bibliographic information for sources.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

Justify opinions or persuade others by providing detailed and relevant textual evidence (e.g., quoting from the text directly or referring to specific textual evidence) or relevant background knowledge, with light support.
Justify opinions by providing some textual evidence (e.g., quoting from the text) or relevant background knowledge, with substantial support.
Justify opinions or persuade others by providing relevant textual evidence (e.g., quoting from the text or referring to what the text says) or relevant background knowledge, with moderate support.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.
